findings.title: Finding 1 (High): client certificates leak process-wide through the shared `_preloaded_ssl_context`
findings.quote:
Priority: High. File: `src/requests/adapters.py`, lines 75-78 (module-level context), 94-95 (`verify is True` installs the shared context into `pool_kwargs`), and 102-109 (`cert_file`/`key_file` placed into the same `pool_kwargs`).

Evidence. `_urllib3_request_context()` hands the single module-level `ssl.SSLContext` to every `verify=True` pool, for every host and every `Session`, because the context object is created once at import and never copied. urllib3 does not treat a caller-supplied context as read-only: in the installed urllib3 2.8.0, `connection.py:876-893` passes `ssl_context=self.ssl_context` together with `cert_file=self.cert_file`/`key_file=self.key_file` into `_ssl_wrap_socket_and_match_hostname()`, which assigns `context.verify_mode` (line 1042) and then calls `ssl_wrap_socket()`, which calls `context.load_cert_chain(certfile, keyfile)` on that same object (`util/ssl_.py:429-433`) on every new connection. The urllib3 pool key includes `cert_file`/`key_file`, so a request with `cert=` gets its own pool, but the pool merely references the same shared context; the pool separation that previously isolated client identities no longer isolates anything. At the merge-base each pool built a fresh context per connection, so a client certificate stayed scoped to the (host, cert) pool that asked for it. I reproduced this offline against a local TLS server that optionally requests a client certificate (trustme-issued CA; the test CA was added to the preloaded context to stand in for a publicly trusted server certificate, and on the merge-base the equivalent tweak was pointing `DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH` at the test CA). Head: after `Session A` sends `get(url, cert=(client-one))`, a brand-new `Session B` calling `get(url)` with no `cert`, and the top-level `requests.get(url)`, both complete the handshake presenting `client-one`'s certificate. Merge-base: the same two requests present no client certificate. The existing suite does not catch this: `test_different_connection_pool_for_mtls_settings` only checks that a certificate was seen on the `verify=False` request and that the `verify=True` request fails, and on this machine it fails at both merge-base and head for the unrelated expired-fixture reason noted above.

Failure / vulnerability. Once any code path in the process performs a `verify=True` request with a client certificate (for example an mTLS call to an internal API), every subsequent default-verified TLS connection in the process, from any `Session` and to any host, answers a server's `CertificateRequest` with that client certificate and a signature made with its private key. That discloses the client identity to third-party servers and performs unintended authentication wherever that certificate is accepted; the application has no way to opt out short of `verify=False` or a custom bundle. Because `load_cert_chain()` and the handshake are not atomic and the context is shared across threads, two concurrent `verify=True` requests carrying different client certificates can also present each other's identity (the PR discussion itself quotes the CPython ssl maintainer that reconfiguring mTLS certificates on an in-use context "can lead to surprising behavior"). The same mechanism means that any `HTTPAdapter` subclass which sets `conn.ca_certs` for `verify=True` (a common corporate-CA pattern) now calls `load_verify_locations()` on the global context and permanently widens the trust store for every other session in the process. Requests with `cert is not None` must not be routed onto `_preloaded_ssl_context` (or must get a per-pool copy of it).

findings.title: Finding 2 (Medium): HTTPS proxies and other pools without the preloaded context now verify against the OS trust store instead of certifi
findings.quote:
Priority: Medium. File: `src/requests/adapters.py`, lines 297-317 (`cert_verify()` no longer sets `conn.ca_certs`/`conn.ca_cert_dir` for `verify=True`).

Evidence. The PR relies on the pool's `ssl_context` to carry the certifi trust store, but urllib3 does not use the pool's `ssl_context` for every TLS handshake the pool performs. For a tunnelled HTTPS proxy (an `https://` proxy URL with an `https://` target, the default tunnelling mode), `HTTPSConnection.connect()` calls `_connect_tls_proxy()` (`connection.py:832-837`), which with requests' default `proxy_config.ssl_context=None` takes the branch `ssl_context = self.ssl_context if self.proxy_is_forwarding else None` and `ca_certs = self.ca_certs` (`connection.py:962-971`). With `ssl_context=None` and `ca_certs=None`, `_ssl_wrap_socket_and_match_hostname()` builds a fresh default context and calls `context.load_default_certs()` (`connection.py:1061-1068`), i.e. the operating-system trust store. At the merge-base `cert_verify()` set `conn.ca_certs` to the certifi bundle, so the proxy handshake loaded certifi and skipped `load_default_certs()`. I confirmed the state difference offline by building the pool through `_get_connection()` + `cert_verify()` with `proxies={'https': 'https://127.0.0.1:9'}`: at head the new connection has `ca_certs=None` and `ca_cert_dir=None`; at the merge-base it has `ca_certs=<default bundle>`. `docs/user/advanced.rst:652-657` documents that the certificates trusted when proxying https connections are those in `DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH`. The same gap applies to any pool that was not created through `_get_connection()`: `get_connection()` is still public and documented for subclassing, and third-party adapters that override `send()` and call `self.get_connection()` followed by `self.cert_verify(conn, url, True, cert)` (the pre-2.32 pattern) now receive a pool with `cert_reqs=CERT_REQUIRED` but no CA configuration, so urllib3 falls back to `load_default_certs()` for them as well.

Failure. `verify=True` requests through an `https://` proxy change trust anchors silently from the certifi bundle to whatever the OS exposes to OpenSSL. On platforms where `load_default_certs()` finds nothing (python.org macOS builds without the "Install Certificates" step, slim or distroless containers without `ca-certificates`), those requests now fail with `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED` where they previously succeeded; on platforms with an OS store the proxy certificate is validated against a different CA set than documented. Users of the documented `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` override are unaffected because that path becomes a string `verify`, which still sets `ca_certs`.

findings.title: Finding 3 (Medium): `import requests` now fails outright when the default CA bundle is missing, empty, or `ssl` is unavailable
findings.quote:
Priority: Medium. File: `src/requests/adapters.py`, lines 75-78.

Evidence. `create_urllib3_context()` and `load_verify_locations(extract_zipped_paths(DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH))` now run at module import. At the merge-base the bundle was only resolved inside `cert_verify()` for an `https` URL with truthy `verify`, and a bad path produced a clear `OSError("Could not find a suitable TLS CA certificate bundle, invalid path: ...")` on that request only. I verified with the pre-provisioned virtualenv: with `certifi.where()` returning a non-existent path, `import requests` at head raises `FileNotFoundError` while the merge-base imports normally; with an empty bundle file, head raises `ssl.SSLError: [X509: NO_CERTIFICATE_OR_CRL_FOUND]` while the merge-base imports normally. `src/requests/__init__.py:119-129` deliberately tolerates a missing `ssl` module, but urllib3 sets `SSLContext = None` when `ssl` is unavailable (`util/ssl_.py:16`) and `create_urllib3_context()` calls `SSLContext(PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT)` (`util/ssl_.py:256`), so such interpreters now fail at import with `TypeError`. The extraction of a zipped bundle (`extract_zipped_paths`) also moves to import time, so a read-only or missing temp directory in a zipapp/PyInstaller deployment fails the import rather than the first verified request. The descriptive error path in `cert_verify()` (lines 308-312) is now reachable only for string `verify` values.

Failure. Environments whose default bundle is broken (distro-patched certifi pointing at `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` in an image without `ca-certificates`, a damaged or zero-length `cacert.pem`, an unwritable temp dir for zipped bundles, or a Python built without `ssl`) go from "verified HTTPS fails with a descriptive error, everything else works" to "the package cannot be imported", taking down plain `http://` usage, `verify=False` usage, custom-bundle usage and anything that merely imports requests transitively. As a side effect, the long-standing workaround of reassigning `requests.adapters.DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH` (or `requests.certs.where`) after import to point at a corporate bundle now silently does nothing for `verify=True`, because the bundle is read exactly once at import and `cert_verify()` no longer consults it.

findings.title: Finding 4 (Low): pyOpenSSL injected after import is bypassed for `verify=True` connections
findings.quote:
Priority: Low. File: `src/requests/adapters.py`, lines 75-78 and 94-95.

Evidence. The preloaded context is whatever `create_urllib3_context()` returns at import time. If `urllib3.contrib.pyopenssl.inject_into_urllib3()` is called after `import requests` (the natural ordering in user scripts; requests' own injection in `__init__.py` happens before `adapters` is imported and so is unaffected), `_preloaded_ssl_context` is a stdlib `ssl.SSLContext`, and urllib3's `ssl_wrap_socket()` uses the supplied context's `wrap_socket()` directly (`util/ssl_.py:437`), so every default-verified connection bypasses pyOpenSSL even though `IS_PYOPENSSL` is true. In that state `_ssl_wrap_socket_and_match_hostname()` also sets `check_hostname = False` on the shared stdlib context (`connection.py:1053-1056`); hostname verification still happens through urllib3's manual `_match_hostname()`, so this is a behaviour change rather than a verification bypass. Connections with `verify=<path>` or `verify=False` still get a fresh context of the injected type, so the TLS implementation now differs between `verify=True` and other modes within the same process.

Failure. Users who rely on pyOpenSSL for `verify=True` traffic (for example for its certificate handling or to work around an OpenSSL build issue) silently get the stdlib implementation instead, and the mixed-implementation behaviour is hard to diagnose because it depends on import order.
